chapters.name: Chapter 1: Know who you are talking to

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Describing your ideal customer
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-paragraph profile of the customer you most want.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI and at least one real customer conversation or sales record, you will write a one-paragraph profile of your ideal customer, with every guess checked against real people.
Marketing to "everyone" reaches no one. Your ideal customer is the person who needs what you sell, can pay for it, and is easy for you to reach. A home bakery's ideal customer might be "busy parents within 10 miles who order birthday cakes two to four times a year."
AI can help you think it through. Tell it what you sell and who buys now, then ask: "Help me describe my ideal customer: their situation, their biggest problem, what they worry about before buying, and where they spend time online."
AI is guessing from general patterns. Check its guesses against real customers: look at who has bought from you, read their messages, and ask three customers why they chose you.
Step by step:
- Write what you sell and who has bought from you so far.
- Ask AI to help describe the ideal customer's situation, problem, worries and where they spend time.
- Check the guesses with three real customers or your sales records.
- Write a one-paragraph profile.
Words to know:
- Ideal customer: the person who most needs what you sell, can pay, and is easy to reach.
- Profile: a short description of a type of customer.
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to draft your ideal-customer profile, then check it against at least one real customer conversation or your sales records. Save the final paragraph.
You can now describe the customer your marketing is for, checked against real people.

options: A short description of the customer you most want to reach
A list of every person in your town
check.why: A profile describes the person your marketing is aimed at.

check.q: AI says your customers mostly use one app, but your sales records show otherwise. What do you do?
options: Go with what your real records show
check.why: Real customers and records beat AI's guesses.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing a clear, honest offer
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence offer that says who it is for, what they get and why it matters.
This lesson builds toward: Given your customer profile, you will write a one-sentence offer that says who it is for, what they get and why it matters, with every claim true and provable.
An offer answers three questions fast: Who is this for? What do they get? Why should they care? Example: "Busy parents in Decatur: custom birthday cakes delivered to your door, so the party is one less thing to worry about."
Give AI your customer profile and ask: "Write five one-sentence offers for this customer. Plain words, no hype." Pick the best and edit it in your own voice.
Keep it honest. In the US the FTC says ads must be truthful, not misleading, and backed by evidence. Do not say "best in town", "guaranteed results" or "AI-powered" unless it is true and you can prove it.
Step by step:
- Paste your customer profile into an AI assistant.
- Ask for five one-sentence offers in plain words.
- Choose one and edit it to sound like you.
- Remove any claim you cannot prove.
Words to know:
- Offer: what you are selling, who it is for and why it matters, said simply.
- Claim: something your ad says is true.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
Try it now: Ask AI for five offers based on your customer profile, choose one, edit it, and check that every claim in it is true and provable.
You can now write a short, honest offer that speaks to your ideal customer.

check.q: What must every claim in your offer be?
check.why: FTC rules require truthful, backed-up claims.

check.q: AI writes "the fastest service in town" but you have no proof. What do you do?
options: Remove it or replace it with something you can prove
check.why: Claims you cannot back up should not go in your offer.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning a month of content
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to build a 12-post content calendar for one month.
This lesson builds toward: Given your offer, you will create a 12-post content calendar for one month with AI, with a mix of post types on one or two platforms your customers use, saved with dates.
Posting three times a week for a month is 12 posts. A simple mix keeps it interesting: teach something useful, show your work or your team, share a customer story (with permission), and make your offer.
Ask AI: "Make a 12-post content calendar for [business] for [customer]. Mix: 4 helpful tips, 3 behind-the-scenes, 2 customer stories, 3 offer posts. Give each a date, a one-line idea and the platform."
Choose platforms where your customer already spends time (from your profile). It is better to post well on one or two platforms than poorly on five.
Step by step:
- Choose one or two platforms where your customer spends time.
- Ask AI for a 12-post calendar with a mix of post types.
- Edit ideas that do not fit your business.
- Put the calendar in a spreadsheet or document with dates.
Words to know:
- Content calendar: a plan that lists what you will post and when.
- Platform: a social media site or app, like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok or LinkedIn.
Try it now: Have AI build your 12-post calendar, edit it to fit your business, and save it with dates in a spreadsheet or document.
You can now plan a month of varied content for the platforms your customers use.

check.q: What does a good content mix include?
options: Tips, behind-the-scenes, customer stories and offers
check.why: A mix keeps people interested and builds trust.

check.q: Your customers are mostly on one platform. Where do you post?
options: Start where your customers already are
Nowhere until you have more time
check.why: One or two platforms where customers already are is enough to start.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Create, publish and follow the rules

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making posts and graphics with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn calendar ideas into finished posts with captions and graphics.
This lesson builds toward: Given three calendar ideas, you will make finished posts with edited AI captions and Canva graphics, using real photos where possible and never faking results.
For each post, ask a chat assistant for a caption: "Write an Instagram caption for this idea: [idea]. For [customer]. Friendly, under 80 words, one question to invite comments, and a call to action." Ask for two or three versions and pick one.
Make the graphic in Canva from a template, using your brand colors. Use your own photos when you can; real photos of your work build trust. If you use an AI-generated image, check it for errors and never make it look like a real customer or a real result you did not deliver.
Under US Copyright Office guidance, purely AI-generated material is not protected by copyright, while your own creative choices and edits can be. If owning your logo or main brand art matters, have a human designer involved and talk to a lawyer.
Step by step:
- Pick a post from your calendar.
- Ask AI for two or three caption versions and choose one.
- Make the graphic in Canva from a template, with your own photo if you can.
- Check spelling, facts and images.
- Save the post ready to publish.
Words to know:
- Caption: the text that goes with a social media post.
- Copyright: the legal right to control copying of a creative work.
Official sources:
- US Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
- US Copyright Office: Part 2 Copyrightability report announcement
Try it now: Turn three ideas from your calendar into finished posts: an AI-helped caption you edited, and a Canva graphic with your own photo where possible.
You can now make finished social posts with AI captions and graphics, without faking results.

check.q: What makes a strong caption request to AI?
options: The idea, the customer, the length and a call to action
check.why: Specific direction gives a caption you can use.

check.q: AI makes a perfect before-and-after photo of a kitchen you did not clean. What do you do?
options: Edit it slightly and post it
Do not use it; use a real photo of your work
check.why: Images must not suggest results you did not deliver.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reviews, testimonials and endorsements: the rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use reviews and paid promotions in a way that follows FTC rules.
This lesson builds toward: When asking for reviews or working with paid promoters, you will write a review request and disclosures that follow FTC rules, asking all customers, offering no reward for good ratings and disclosing every paid connection.
Real customer reviews are powerful marketing. Fake ones are illegal. The FTC's rule on fake reviews bans creating, buying or selling fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-generated reviews that pretend to come from people who do not exist. It also bans offering a reward only for positive reviews.
You CAN ask happy and unhappy customers alike to leave an honest review, and you can share real reviews with permission. Do not use AI to write reviews, and do not edit a review to change its meaning.
If you pay or give free products to someone to promote you, the connection must be disclosed clearly, such as "#ad" or "Sponsored" at the start of the post, and in the video itself for videos. You are responsible for what your promoters say for you.
Step by step:
- Ask all customers for honest reviews, not just happy ones.
- Share real reviews only with permission and without changing their meaning.
- Never use AI to write reviews.
- Make anyone you pay or gift disclose it clearly, like "#ad" at the start.
Words to know:
- Testimonial: a customer's statement about your business used in marketing.
- Endorsement: a message that people will think shows someone else's honest opinion, like an influencer's post.
- Disclose: tell people clearly.
Official sources:
- FTC: Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (press release)
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
Try it now: Use AI to draft a short, honest message asking recent customers for a review (not just happy ones, and no reward for a good rating). Edit and save it.
You can now collect and use reviews and paid promotions the honest, legal way.

check.q: Which review request follows FTC rules?
options: Asking all recent customers for an honest review
Offering a discount only for five-star reviews
check.why: Asking everyone for honest reviews, with no reward for good ratings, is allowed.

check.q: A friend gets free products to post about your shop. What do you ask them to do?
options: Clearly disclose it, such as "#ad" at the start
check.why: Paid or gifted connections must be clearly disclosed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a marketing email that follows CAN-SPAM
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a marketing email with AI that meets the CAN-SPAM basics.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI to draft a marketing email, you will check the email against the CAN-SPAM basics, with an honest subject line, your physical address and a working unsubscribe line.
Email reaches people who already know you. Ask AI: "Write a short marketing email to past customers of [business] about [offer]. Friendly, under 150 words, one clear call to action, and three honest subject line options."
In the US, the CAN-SPAM Act covers commercial email. The FTC's guide lists the basics: accurate "From" information, a subject line that is not deceptive, making clear it is an ad, your valid physical postal address, and a clear way to opt out. You must honor opt-out requests within 10 business days. Penalties can be large per email, so check the FTC page.
Only email people who gave you their address and agreed to hear from you, and use an email service that handles unsubscribes for you. Other countries have their own rules; check them if you email customers abroad.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for the email and three honest subject lines.
- Check every fact and claim.
- Make sure it shows your business name, your physical address and an unsubscribe link.
- Send only to people who agreed to hear from you.
- Honor opt-outs within 10 business days.
Words to know:
- CAN-SPAM Act: the US law with rules for commercial (marketing) email.
- Opt out: ask to stop getting messages; unsubscribe.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: Final task: write your marketing email with AI, check it against the CAN-SPAM basics (honest subject, ad identified, address, unsubscribe), and put it together with your profile, offer, calendar and three posts as your one-month marketing pack.
You can now plan, create and send honest marketing that follows US advertising and email rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Ideal customer Too broad, such as "everyone", or not checked against real customers. One paragraph on who they are, their problem and where they spend time, checked against real people. Notes which AI guesses were wrong and fixed. Offer Missing who, what or why, or includes a claim that cannot be proven. One sentence with who it is for, what they get and why it matters, all true. Uses the customer's own words from a real conversation. Content calendar Fewer than 12 posts, no dates, or one post type only. 12 dated posts with a mix of types on one or two platforms. Each post links to the offer or the customer's problem. Finished posts Captions unedited, or images suggest results not delivered. Three posts with edited captions, graphics and a call to action, honest images. Uses real photos of the owner's work, with permission for any customer shown. Rule-following email Missing an honest subject, the address or the unsubscribe line. Honest subject, identified as an ad, physical address and working unsubscribe. Also notes how unsubscribes will be handled within 10 business days. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What must a CAN-SPAM marketing email include?
check.why: CAN-SPAM requires a valid physical postal address.

check.q: You bought a list of email addresses from a stranger. What do you do?
options: Add them to your newsletter quietly
Do not use it; email only people who agreed
check.why: Send marketing email to people who gave you their address and agreed.
